source_version: Journal de l’École polytechnique — Mathématiques 11 (2024), publisher version, DOI 10.5802/jep.253, pp. 187–246
purpose: Record the exact hypotheses, quantifiers, objects, normalisations and limits of the retained unit, and what the file does not settle, so a later reader cannot quietly strengthen a hypothesis or drop a normalisation. No correctness judgement, no formula repair, no added hypothesis.
hypotheses_as_written: R is a semilocal Prüfer domain with fraction field K. Prüfer means every local ring is a valuation ring; semilocal is part of the hypothesis, not derived.

A is an integral, semilocal, and essentially smooth R-algebra. 'Essentially smooth' is used in the paper's own sense; the notations subsection (native 399-416) fixes Frac, localisation notation and the reductive-group convention, and 'essentially smooth' occurs in the body at 1007 and inside 3.5 and 8.2. 'Integral' and 'semilocal' are separate hypotheses and both are used.
G is a quasi-split reductive A-group scheme. Quasi-split is required for clause (ii) as well, and is not weakened to 'G has a Borel after a finite étale cover'.
Clause (i) is stated over A ⊗_R K, i.e. for the generic R-fibre, and does not assume dim R = 1.
Clause (ii) adds exactly one hypothesis: R has Krull dimension 1. Nothing else about R is strengthened (in particular R need not be Noetherian, excellent, or of finite rank as a valuation ring).
'Generically trivial' means trivial over Frac A, i.e. the torsor lies in the kernel of the displayed restriction map; the conclusion is that this kernel is the single point set {*}.
conclusion_as_written: Clause (i): Ker(H^1_ét(A ⊗_R K, G) → H^1_ét(Frac A, G)) = {*}.
Clause (ii): Ker(H^1_ét(A, G) → H^1_ét(Frac A, G)) = {*}.
Both are stated as equalities of the kernel with the one-point set, not as injectivity of a map between pointed sets; they say every generically trivial torsor IS trivial.
The proof does not re-prove the underlying toral purity and Grothendieck-Serre inputs: it invokes the paper's own 7.9 and 7.11 (with 3.2, 3.4, 3.5, 6.6) and closes by \cite[Th.\,5.1]{GL23}.

objects_that_must_not_be_confused.name: clause (i) and clause (ii)
objects_that_must_not_be_confused.why_it_matters: (i) is a statement about the generic fibre A ⊗_R K with no dimension hypothesis; (ii) is a statement about A itself and is where dim R = 1 is consumed. Reading (i) as already containing (ii)'s hypothesis, or (ii) as valid for arbitrary Prüfer R, changes the theorem.

objects_that_must_not_be_confused.name: Prüfer domain vs valuation ring
objects_that_must_not_be_confused.why_it_matters: the paper's base is a semilocal Prüfer domain; several reduction lemmas (8.3-8.7) are applied after passing to a finite-rank valuation ring, and the intermediate objects (X over V, points x with d_x = dim O_{X_s,x}) are not the theorem's own objects.

objects_that_must_not_be_confused.name: the toral purity 7.9 and the toral Grothendieck-Serre 7.11
objects_that_must_not_be_confused.why_it_matters: both are stated for groups of multiplicative type, and 7.11 needs a connected finite étale Galois cover splitting M. Neither is a statement about reductive G; they are inputs, and 8.1 does not inherit their hypotheses verbatim.

objects_that_must_not_be_confused.name: Lemma 8.4 and its external source
objects_that_must_not_be_confused.why_it_matters: 8.4 is quoted from \cite[Lem.\,5.1]{Ces22a}, whose original statement assumed A Noetherian; the author notes at 2272 that Noetherianness was not used. The leaner hypothesis (semilocal with geometrically unibranch local rings) is the one actually used and is recorded as the author states it, without this unit asserting the validity of the removal.

objects_that_must_not_be_confused.name: the relative curve C and A^1_A
objects_that_must_not_be_confused.why_it_matters: the reduction replaces C by an étale neighbourhood, then by a curve with a flat map to A^1_A, then by A^1_A itself via patching; Z is replaced accordingly at each step. Only the final configuration (C = A^1_A, s = 0, (G,B) = (G_C, B_C)) is what the closing "section theorem" applies to.

normalisation_points: The Borel B of the quasi-split G is fixed once and for all in 8.3, and the quasi-pinnings are part of the data carried through 8.3-8.7 ('compatible with the quasi-pinnings' in clauses 1iii/1iv and 2iii/2iv).
In 8.7 the section is normalised to s = 0 in A^1_A(A) by a shift; this shift is the author's, and the statement of 8.1 does not mention any section.

In the closing proof the closed subscheme Z is enlarged (at author's line 2330) to make A^1_A \ Z affine, using that any A-finite closed subscheme of A^1_A lies in {f = 0} for a monic f in A[t]. This enlargement is part of the proof, not of the statement.
The relative dimension d ≥ 1 and the point x with d_x = dim O_{X_s,x} belong to the intermediate geometric setting of 8.2/3.5 and never appear in 8.1.
limits_and_uniformity: No bound in 8.1 is uniform in R, A or G: the theorem is a vanishing statement, not a quantitative one.

Clause (ii) genuinely needs dim R = 1; the author states at 367-375 that the geometric input 8.2 'unfortunately' imposes this constraint, so the dimension-1 hypothesis is a limitation of the method as the author describes it, not a conjectural sharpness claim.
Semilocality of R and of A is used through the limit lemma 3.4 and the punctured-spectrum quasi-compactness that comes with it; nothing here says the result holds for a general Prüfer domain.

The paper's more general purity theorems (6.3, 6.5, 6.8, 6.9, 7.9, 7.11) are stated under their own hypotheses (S-flat with regular fibres, finite-rank valuation ring, coaffine étale locally, groups of multiplicative type) and must not be folded into 8.1.
what_the_file_does_not_settle: Whether 8.1 is a new theorem or a Prüferian specialisation of \cite{Ces22a} (with earlier version \cite{Fed22b}): the author says at 367-375 and 2135-2136 that the proof follows the same strategy as Ces22a, and at 2136-2137 that clause (i) is a version of the Nisnevich conjecture inspired by \cite[Th.\,1.3(2)]{Ces22b}, which treats Dedekind R. The novelty question is left to the owner decision recorded in DIFFICULTY_SCREENING.json; this unit does not assert it either way.
Whether the geometric input 8.2 (a consequence of \cite[Prop.\,4.1]{Ces22a}) holds for R of dimension > 1: the author explicitly says the dimension-1 restriction comes from here.

Whether 6.5, 6.8, 6.9 hold for X merely flat and locally finitely presented with regular fibres: the author records this as anticipated but not confirmed, at 1759-1761 after 6.8 and at 1839-1840 after 6.9, because the method relies on Auslander's criterion, which needs smoothness.
Nothing in the file computes or bounds the size of H^1_ét(A, G) beyond the vanishing of the generic-triviality kernel.
